title: From Chicago's Michelin Star to Phoenix and Hudson Yards: The Sujan Sarkar Playbook
excerpt: The Kolkata-born chef behind Indienne is building a multi-city, multi-concept Indian restaurant empire — and mentoring the next generation of desi chefs along the way.
body:
Chef Sujan Sarkar does not believe in doing just one thing well. The Kolkata-born, London-trained chef behind Chicago's Michelin-starred Indienne now oversees a growing portfolio of Indian restaurants spanning multiple cities and culinary philosophies — and his latest moves signal a national ambition that could reshape how America eats Indian food.

## NADU Heads West

NADU, Sarkar's regional Indian restaurant that debuted in Chicago's Lincoln Park in April 2025, is preparing to open its second location at Desert Ridge Marketplace in North Phoenix. The 4,024-square-foot space, located at 21001 N. Tatum Blvd., will accommodate more than 120 guests and feature a contemporary design inspired by modern India, including artwork from Chicago-based artist Abhay Sehgal.

The Chicago original earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand designation and a James Beard Award semifinalist nomination for Best New Restaurant within its first year — a remarkable run for a concept built around the idea that Indian cuisine is not one cuisine but dozens. The menu spans Tangra Chili Fish from Kolkata's Chinese-Indian quarter, Kerala-style beef ularthiyathu, Dadar Vada Pav from Mumbai's street stalls, and Kashmiri Roganjosh — each dish labelled with its region of origin.

"This is not Indian cuisine, rather it's cuisines of India," Sarkar has said. "There are so many micro cuisines in India, and we want to showcase them in ways that are as close to their traditional form as possible."

The Phoenix location will be led by Executive Chef Pujan Sarkar, Sujan's brother and longtime mentee, who also helms Tiya, a Michelin-recognised Indian tasting-menu restaurant in San Francisco. To bring the Arizona outpost to life, the team partnered with Zest Hospitality Group, the operators behind Feringhee Modern Indian Cuisine in Chandler.

## Indienne Lands in New York

But Phoenix is only half the story. This spring, Sarkar brought a second Indienne to Hudson Yards in Manhattan — a move that puts his progressive Indian tasting-menu concept in direct conversation with New York's fiercely competitive fine-dining scene.

The original Indienne, which opened in Chicago's River North in 2022, now does 650 to 670 covers a week. It was the first Indian restaurant in Chicago to earn a Michelin star, and has collected James Beard Award nominations in 2024 and 2025, plus recognition from *Bon Appétit*, *Esquire*, and the *Wine Spectator*.

Sarkar's approach at Indienne melds Indian flavours with French techniques — a reflection of his years cooking in London's fine-dining kitchens before moving to the United States. The restaurant now offers a fully vegan tasting menu and a nonalcoholic beverage pairing, additions that Sarkar frames as evolution rather than compromise.

## The Mentorship Model

What truly distinguishes Sarkar from other celebrity chefs is his growth model. Rather than stamping his name on every door, he partners with younger chefs to create distinct concepts. Sifr, a Middle Eastern restaurant, was launched with Sahil Sethi. Swadesi, a South Asian bakery and café celebrating India's chai culture, was built with Yash Kishinchand. NADU itself was developed with head chef Sanchit Sahu, an Odisha-born veteran of Taj Hotels who previously worked at ROOH in New Delhi and JHOL in Bangkok.

"In India if I do a homestyle restaurant, it's like, *why am I eating homestyle food outside of my house?*" Sahu has said. "But here in America, people miss home."

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans who have watched their cuisine be reduced to butter chicken and naan at suburban strip malls, Sarkar's ascent represents something deeper. This is not fusion. It is not "elevated" in the patronising sense that word is sometimes used. It is an Indian chef in America, cooking Indian food on Indian terms, and being rewarded by the most established institutions in Western gastronomy.

The expansion also signals a business maturity that the Indian restaurant scene in America has lacked. Where most successful Indian restaurants remain single-location operations, Sarkar is building replicable concepts — each distinct, each led by a capable chef, each funded to compete in prime real estate markets from Lincoln Park to Hudson Yards to Desert Ridge.

The model invites a question: can an Indian chef build a Joël Robuchon-scale portfolio in America? With five concepts across three cities, two Michelin recognitions, and a James Beard track record, Sarkar is closer to answering yes than anyone before him.
